item.title: Ep 2 – Trust the numbers you measure yourself (19 Oct 2026)
item.description:
The numbers on the label versus the numbers you measure yourself: vendor benchmarks, grid connections and benchmark coverage. Three stories, plus this week's roadmap deep dive.

  • DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 model card (Hugging Face): open weights under MIT, 763B parameters; on DeepSeek's own table, DeepSWE 77.0 vs Opus 5's 74.0, Terminal-Bench 4.0 up from 31.2 to 42.3 (Opus 5: 51.8). HN discussion.
  • DeepSeek Search & Fetch API docs: search with relevance scores and authority tiers, fetch as Markdown, US$0.75 per 1,000 successful requests, 5 QPS each. HN discussion.
  • Microsoft pulls out of AI datacentre project in Essex over power supply concerns (The Guardian) and BBC News: Nscale's £2bn Loughton site loses its anchor tenant; UK Power Networks can't supply enough power until the early to mid-2030s.
  • A benchmark map of the US economy (Mercor): 29 benchmarks mapped to 923 occupations and 18,797 O*NET tasks; an estimated 90% of US working hours go to tasks with little or no benchmark coverage. HN discussion.
  • Week 1 deep dive: AI Evals: Everything You Need to Know (FAQ) by Hamel Husain and Shreya Shankar, and Error Analysis: The First Eval You Should Run (AgentEngineering.org, source of the Nurture Boss example).

Narrated by William and Natasha. Music: original, synthesised for this show.

This week's learning tip – Week 1: Error analysis, look at your data first

Theme: Phase 1 (Prove it works) begins. Before picking any eval tool or metric, read your own agent traces, note the first thing that went wrong in each, and count the failure modes.

Why it matters: every serious eval practice starts with reading traces and counting failures, not with picking a tool. People who skip this build generic metrics that measure nothing. The counts tell you which failures deserve a cheap code assertion, which need a binary LLM judge, and which you should just fix today.

Resources:

  • AI Evals: Everything You Need to Know (FAQ) by Hamel Husain and Shreya Shankar (updated Sept 2026). Read "Getting Started & Fundamentals" and "Error Analysis & Data Collection".
  • Error Analysis: The First Eval You Should Run on AgentEngineering.org: a tight walkthrough of open coding, axial coding and counting, with three small stdlib Python scripts (sampling, tallying, judge checking).

Hands-on (about 2–3 hours):

  • Export 60–100 traces from one of your real agents, ideally the MCP + Codex integration. If production data is sensitive, generate synthetic traces using the FAQ's "dimensions → tuples → queries" method.
  • Get Codex to build a tiny trace-review app in under an hour, with keyboard shortcuts, a notes field and a pass/fail button.
  • Open-code 30 traces yourself, noting the first thing that went wrong in each.
  • Cluster the notes into 4–8 failure modes and count them.

Deliverable: failure_taxonomy.md covering each failure mode, its count, an example trace and a suspected fix, plus the review app, committed to your agent-reliability-lab repo. Keep anything AirTrunk-confidential out and use synthetic or sanitised data.

Transcript

William: G'day Javier. I'm William.

Natasha: And I'm Natasha. This is Javier's AI Daily, Monday the nineteenth of October.

William: One thread today: the numbers on the label, versus the numbers you have to measure yourself.

* * *

William: [STORY 1 – DEEPSEEK]

Natasha: Over the weekend, a "minor update" lit up Hacker News. DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, version ten-seventeen. Open weights, MIT licence, seven hundred and sixty-three billion parameters.

William: And on DeepSeek's own table, it beats Opus 5 on DeepSWE, seventy-seven to seventy-four.

Natasha: Terminal-Bench jumped from thirty-one to forty-two, though Opus 5 still leads there at almost fifty-two. DeepSeek says it also finishes tasks faster, with shorter outputs.

William: And the weekend's biggest Hacker News story was DeepSeek's new Search and Fetch APIs for agents. Search returns structured results with a relevance score and an authority tier. Fetch returns a page as Markdown. Seventy-five cents per thousand successful requests, and empty results or timeouts aren't billed.

Natasha: Why this matters to you: those scores come from DeepSeek, in harnesses DeepSeek chose. A cheaper model is only a win once your own eval set proves it holds up on your tasks.

* * *

Natasha: [STORY 2 – NSCALE AND MICROSOFT]

William: Loughton, Essex. UK ministers called it the country's largest sovereign AI data centre. In March, the site was still a working scaffolding yard.

Natasha: And this weekend we learned it has lost its anchor tenant.

William: Microsoft has pulled out of Nscale's two-billion-pound project. It was the only publicly announced customer for the site.

Natasha: The reason is power. UK Power Networks told Nscale it can't supply enough electricity until the early to mid twenty-thirties. Nscale says it's still committed, and is exploring generating power on site.

William: It's also a blow to Nscale's hopes of a Wall Street float at a potential thirty-five billion dollar valuation. Microsoft declined to comment.

Natasha: Why this matters to you: in your industry the scarce input isn't chips or land. It's a grid connection with a date on it. When you size AI workloads, start from megawatts and energisation dates.

* * *

Natasha: [STORY 3 – MERCOR BENCHMARK MAP]

Natasha: Here's an uncomfortable number. Ninety percent.

William: That's Mercor's estimate of how much American working time goes on tasks that AI benchmarks barely cover, if at all.

Natasha: They mapped twenty-nine agentic benchmarks onto the US Labor Department's taxonomy of nine hundred and twenty-three occupations and almost nineteen thousand tasks. Only two hundred and eight occupations had a task with at least five benchmark prompts.

William: Coverage is lopsided. Lawyers' tasks are heavily tested. Legal secretaries and court clerks, barely. And the tagging was done by an LLM judge, which they checked against human expert labels.

Natasha: Why this matters to you: no public leaderboard measures MCP tool calls under Entra scopes. If you want to know whether a model is good at your work, you build that benchmark yourself.

* * *

William: Which is this week's deep dive. Week one of your roadmap: error analysis.

Natasha: One property-management company read its own assistant's conversations and found it failing two-thirds of the time on dates like "next Tuesday". After categorising, testing and measuring, date handling went from thirty-three to ninety-five percent.

William: Your version: export sixty to a hundred traces from your MCP and Codex agent, and get Codex to build a tiny review app.

Natasha: Open-code thirty traces yourself, noting only the first thing that went wrong. Then cluster the notes into four to eight failure modes, and count them.

William: The deliverable is a failure taxonomy file. The reading list is in the episode description.

Natasha: Have a great week, Javier.

William: See you tomorrow.

item.title: Ep 1 – Agents are outrunning our tools (16 Oct 2026)
item.description:
Agents now write code faster than teams can review or secure it. Three stories, each with why it matters to you.

  • Redesigning source control at Anthropic: 2,500 to 30,000+ merges a day; a 7-person team built Scion, an API-first, server-side VCS, in five months.
  • AI coding agents generate more code, but not more software (Ars Technica): Harvard study of 700+ firms, ~30% more code, no change in features shipped, review time +49%.
  • AI agents aren't going rogue: frontier labs are skipping security basics (CSO Online): sandboxing, egress control and monitoring.
  • Coach's tip reading: evals FAQ by Hamel Husain and Shreya Shankar.

Narrated by William and Natasha. Music: original, synthesised for this show.

Transcript

William: G'day Javier. I'm William.

Natasha: And I'm Natasha. This is Javier's AI Daily, Friday the sixteenth of October.

William: Three stories today, one thread: agents now write code faster than our tools, our reviewers and our security can keep up.

* * *

William: [STORY 1 – ANTHROPIC SOURCE CONTROL]

Natasha: Picture a CI fleet doing twenty-five million code checkouts a day. Several hundred git mirrors, straining. And every week, the number of merges keeps climbing.

William: That was Anthropic this year. In May they merged about two and a half thousand changes a day. By September, more than thirty thousand.

Natasha: Git was built for humans working offline, every clone a full copy. But almost all of Anthropic's clients are agents and CI jobs, and they're always online.

William: So a team of seven built a new system, called Scion, in five months. The server does the heavy lifting: history, blame, diffs, merges, even commits. Clients keep a small cache and fetch only what they need. And every query is an API, so many jobs never check out code at all.

Natasha: The infrastructure is two hundred times smaller than their old mirrors, and checkouts take seconds, not minutes. And the engineers say a big part of their job became telling the model "no", and reviewing the intent of a change rather than every line.

William: Why this matters to you: when your consumers become agents, design for always-online, API-first, incremental access. That's integration architecture, which is your home turf.

* * *

William: [STORY 2 – HARVARD STUDY]

William: Here's a puzzle. Give seven hundred software firms AI coding agents. Code output jumps thirty percent. Commits, pull requests, all up.

Natasha: And the number of features actually shipped doesn't move. Not in any statistically meaningful way.

William: That's from Harvard researchers Fiona Chen and James Stratton, covered by Ars Technica. The missing productivity went into review. Time from pull request to merge rose forty-nine percent.

Natasha: Pull requests needing changes nearly doubled. And although most firms used AI review tools, agents wrote under a quarter of the review comments. The data stops in March, and tools have improved since, but the direction is clear.

William: Why this matters to you: generating code is cheap now. Verifying it is the bottleneck. Engineers who can measure agent quality with evals and golden datasets are the ones who turn more code into more shipped software.

* * *

William: [STORY 3 – AGENT SECURITY]

Natasha: One recent incident went on for days. An AI model, reaching into systems it was never meant to touch. And nobody noticed.

William: The headlines called it agents "going rogue". The security experts CSO Online spoke to had a blunter word: basics.

Natasha: Sandboxes configured badly. No real egress control, so nothing stopped traffic leaving the test environment. And thin monitoring.

William: Why this matters to you: when you wire agents in through MCP and Entra, you decide what they can reach. Give each agent a scoped, least-privilege identity, deny outbound traffic by default, and log every tool call somewhere someone actually looks.

* * *

Natasha: Your coach's tip. Week one of your roadmap starts Monday. Pull your agent traces, read thirty yourself, and note the first thing that went wrong in each.

William: Then group those notes into four to eight failure types. That's your failure taxonomy, and everything in phase one builds on it.

Natasha: Have a great weekend, Javier.

William: See you Monday.
